notes: Our own index of instruments relevant to AI across 11 jurisdictions, reviewed 2026-09. Each entry links to the primary source and is tagged by how binding it is, because a voluntary standard and an Act of Parliament are not the same kind of object however similar their contents look. Not legal advice, not a compliance checklist, and not exhaustive. Instruments that never mention AI are included where they apply to it, which is most of the list in most jurisdictions.

records.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act)
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: The only horizontal AI statute in force anywhere. Bans a short list of practices, imposes conformity assessment on high-risk uses, sets transparency duties on systems people interact with, and adds obligations for general-purpose models above 1e25 FLOP of training compute. It applies in stages rather than at once, and those stages have since moved.

records.title: Digital Omnibus on AI
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Amends the AI Act, in force from July 2026, six days before the high-risk obligations were due to bite. Stand-alone high-risk systems move to December 2027 and systems embedded in regulated products to August 2028. The Article 50 transparency duties were not delayed. Treat any compliance date published before July 2026 as out of date.

records.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation)
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Predates the AI Act and reaches further in practice. Article 22 restricts decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or similarly significant effects, and it is the provision most European automated-decision disputes are actually fought under.

records.title: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act)
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Systemic-risk assessment and mitigation duties on very large platforms and search engines, explicitly including risks from recommender and generative features. Where a model ships inside a large platform, this usually binds before the AI Act does.

records.title: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on liability for defective products
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Brings software and AI systems inside the product liability regime and eases the burden of proof where a claimant could not reasonably be expected to explain how a complex system failed. The separate AI Liability Directive was withdrawn in 2025, so this is what remains.

records.title: Directive (EU) 2019/790 on copyright in the Digital Single Market
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Article 4 permits text and data mining of lawfully accessible works unless the rightsholder reserved the right in a machine-readable way. That reservation is the legal basis for most European objections to training on web data.

records.title: European AI Office
records.force_meaning: Binds government agencies only, not the wider market.
records.note: Supervises general-purpose model obligations directly rather than leaving them to national authorities. It is the only body anywhere with statutory supervisory powers aimed specifically at frontier models.

records.title: General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
records.force_meaning: Guidance with no legal force. Compliance is a choice.
records.note: Voluntary, but signing it is the route to presumed conformity with the AI Act's general-purpose model obligations. A voluntary instrument with that consequence sits between guidance and regulation, which is why it is indexed.

records.title: Framework Act on the Development of AI and Establishment of Trust
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.body: National Assembly of the Republic of Korea
records.note: In force from January 2026. Duties on high-impact AI in listed sectors, labelling of generative output, and a domestic representative requirement for large foreign providers. Administrative fines were given a grace period of about a year, so the obligations bind before the penalties do. Cited in the CSET translation, because Korea's own statute database returns no stable English URL.

records.title: Personal Information Protection Act
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.body: National Assembly of the Republic of Korea
records.note: Includes a right to refuse or seek an explanation of a fully automated decision, added in 2023. Enforced by the Personal Information Protection Commission, which has been among the more active regulators on generative AI.

records.title: Korea AI Safety Institute
records.force_meaning: Binds government agencies only, not the wider market.
records.note: National evaluation capacity, established alongside the framework Act. Korea is one of a small number of jurisdictions with both a horizontal AI statute and a body able to test models against it.

records.title: Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services
records.force_meaning: Rules, regulations or codes made under an Act. Binding.
records.body: Cyberspace Administration of China and six other bodies
records.note: The first binding national rules addressed to generative AI anywhere: security assessment and algorithm filing before public launch, content obligations, and duties on training data.

records.title: Provisions on Deep Synthesis Internet Information Services
records.force_meaning: Rules, regulations or codes made under an Act. Binding.
records.note: Required labelling of synthetic media two years before any comparable Western obligation, and requires consent before generating a likeness of a real person.

records.title: Measures for Labelling AI-Generated Synthetic Content
records.force_meaning: Rules, regulations or codes made under an Act. Binding.
records.body: Cyberspace Administration of China and three other bodies
records.note: In force from September 2025, with a mandatory national standard alongside it. Requires both a label the reader can see and one embedded in file metadata, which is a stronger requirement than the EU's Article 50.

records.title: Provisions on Algorithmic Recommendation of Internet Information Services
records.force_meaning: Rules, regulations or codes made under an Act. Binding.
records.note: Created the algorithm filing regime that the later measures build on, and gave users a right to switch recommendation off. The filing register is the closest thing any jurisdiction has to a public inventory of deployed systems.

records.title: Personal Information Protection Law
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: China's general data protection statute, including rules on automated decision-making and a right to an explanation where a decision has a significant effect on an individual.

records.title: Data Security Law
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Classifies data by importance and restricts cross-border transfer of important data, which constrains where training corpora can be assembled and processed.

records.title: Cybersecurity Law
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: The statute the administrative measures are made under. Network operators carry security obligations and a real-name requirement, which is what makes the algorithm filing and security assessment regimes enforceable.

records.title: Executive Order 14179, Removing Barriers to American Leadership in AI
records.force_meaning: Binds government agencies only, not the wider market.
records.note: Revoked Executive Order 14110 and reset federal policy toward removing regulatory barriers. Executive orders bind the executive branch, not the market, and a successor can revoke them in a day, as this one did.

records.title: Executive Order 14110, Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI (revoked)
records.force_meaning: An inquiry or review. Evidence and recommendations, not obligations.
records.note: Listed because it is still widely cited as current US policy and is not. It introduced the 1e26 FLOP reporting threshold, the second compute threshold written into any official instrument, and was revoked in January 2025.

records.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Criminalises publication of non-consensual intimate imagery including AI-generated depictions, and requires covered platforms to remove it on notice. One of very few federal statutes that names AI-generated material at all.

records.title: Federal Trade Commission Act, section 5
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: The general prohibition on unfair or deceptive acts and practices. With no AI statute in place it is the main federal hook for AI claims that do not hold up, and the FTC has used it against several AI products.

records.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
records.force_meaning: Guidance with no legal force. Compliance is a choice.
records.body: National Institute of Standards and Technology
records.note: No legal force, and the most widely adopted AI governance document in the United States. State bills and procurement rules incorporate it by reference, which is how a voluntary framework acquires teeth.

records.title: California SB 53, Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: State law, and the first binding frontier-model transparency statute anywhere: developers above a compute threshold must publish a safety framework and report critical safety incidents. It reaches most frontier labs because most of them are in California.

records.title: Colorado SB24-205, Artificial Intelligence Act
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: The first US state statute imposing duties on developers and deployers of high-risk AI in consequential decisions. Its commencement date has been amended more than once; check the current one before relying on it.

records.title: Advanced computing and semiconductor export controls
records.force_meaning: Rules, regulations or codes made under an Act. Binding.
records.body: Bureau of Industry and Security, Department of Commerce
records.note: The most materially binding AI rules the United States has, and the least discussed as AI policy. They restrict which accelerators can be sold where, which decides who can train large models at all.

records.title: Act on Promotion of Research, Development and Utilization of AI-Related Technologies
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: In full effect from September 2025. It is a promotion statute: it establishes an AI Strategy Headquarters, sets out a basic plan and assigns roles, and creates no prohibitions and no monetary penalties. Japan has an AI Act and does not have AI obligations, and both halves of that matter.

records.title: Act on the Protection of Personal Information
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: The binding constraint on AI systems handling personal data in Japan, enforced by the Personal Information Protection Commission. Where the AI Act creates no duties, this one does.

records.title: Copyright Act, Article 30-4
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: One of the most permissive text and data mining provisions in the world: use of a work for machine learning is generally permitted where it is not for enjoying the expression itself. The Agency for Cultural Affairs has since narrowed how widely it reads that, which is what the linked guidance covers.

records.title: AI Guidelines for Business
records.force_meaning: Guidance with no legal force. Compliance is a choice.
records.body: Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, and Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications
records.note: The practical governance expectation on Japanese developers and deployers, covering the whole lifecycle. Voluntary, and in a jurisdiction with a penalty-free AI Act it does most of the work.

records.title: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation
records.force_meaning: Guidance with no legal force. Compliance is a choice.
records.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
records.note: The white paper setting out the decision not to legislate horizontally, and to have existing regulators apply five cross-sectoral principles inside their own remits instead. Everything else in this list follows from it.

records.title: Data Protection Act 2018
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: With the UK GDPR, the binding constraint on most AI systems processing personal data, including the restriction on solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.

records.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Relaxes the automated-decision rules outside special-category data, moving from a general prohibition toward a safeguards model. The direction of travel is opposite to the EU's, which matters to anyone assuming the two regimes still track each other.

records.title: Online Safety Act 2023
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Duties of care on user-to-user and search services, enforced by Ofcom. Generative AI chatbots that let users share content fall inside scope, which is the main route by which UK law reaches consumer AI products.

records.title: Equality Act 2010
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: The indirect discrimination provisions apply to automated decisions without naming them. In a jurisdiction with no AI statute, this is what an unfair hiring or credit model is most likely to be challenged under.

records.title: AI Security Institute
records.force_meaning: Binds government agencies only, not the wider market.
records.body: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
records.note: State capacity to test frontier models, established before any comparable body elsewhere and renamed from AI Safety Institute in 2025. It cannot compel access: testing happens by agreement with developers.

records.title: ICO guidance on AI and data protection
records.force_meaning: How a regulator states it will apply existing law. Creates no obligations of its own.
records.note: How the data regulator says it will apply existing law to AI. Not law, and the closest thing to an operational compliance standard the UK has.

records.title: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: The federal private-sector privacy statute, and with provincial equivalents the main binding constraint on commercial AI in Canada. Its reform was bundled into the same bill as the AI statute, so both fell together.

records.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making
records.force_meaning: Binds government agencies only, not the wider market.
records.note: Requires an Algorithmic Impact Assessment before a federal department deploys an automated decision system, with obligations scaled to the assessed impact level. The first instrument of its kind anywhere and still among the most concrete, and it binds government rather than the market.

records.title: Bill C-27, Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (died on the order paper)
records.force_meaning: An inquiry or review. Evidence and recommendations, not obligations.
records.note: Would have been the second comprehensive national AI statute after the EU's. It died when Parliament was prorogued in January 2025 and has not been reintroduced. Listed because it is still frequently cited as Canadian law.

records.title: Voluntary Code of Conduct on Advanced Generative AI Systems
records.force_meaning: Guidance with no legal force. Compliance is a choice.
records.body: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
records.note: Signed by a list of named Canadian developers. With the statute gone this is the operative federal expectation of generative AI developers, and it carries no consequence for ignoring it.

records.title: Lei 13.709/2018 (Lei Geral de Protecao de Dados)
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Brazil's data protection statute, closely modelled on the GDPR, including a right to review of decisions taken solely on automated processing. Enforced by the ANPD, which is also the proposed AI supervisor.

records.title: PL 2338/2023 (Marco Legal da Inteligencia Artificial)
records.force_meaning: Proposed, consulted on, or before Parliament. Creates no duties yet.
records.note: Risk-tiered like the EU AI Act, with additions the EU does not have: rights for affected people, and remuneration for copyright holders whose works are used in training. Passed the Senate in December 2024 and is still before the Chamber of Deputies. It creates no duties yet.

records.title: Lei 12.965/2014 (Marco Civil da Internet)
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: The internet civil rights framework, including platform liability. A 2025 Supreme Court ruling narrowed its safe harbour, which changes the exposure of any platform hosting AI-generated content in Brazil.

records.title: Lei 8.078/1990 (Codigo de Defesa do Consumidor)
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Strict supplier liability for defective products and services. Where an AI product causes harm to a consumer in Brazil, this applies now and does not wait for the AI bill.

records.title: Privacy Act 1988
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: The main constraint on AI systems that handle personal information. The Australian Privacy Principles apply to collection, use and disclosure regardless of whether a model is involved, which is why an Australian AI compliance question is usually a privacy question first.

records.title: Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: The first tranche of reform from the Privacy Act Review. Creates a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy, and requires privacy policies to disclose where personal information is used in automated decisions that significantly affect someone. The automated-decision transparency duty is the closest thing Australia has to an AI transparency obligation, and it commences in December 2026.

records.title: Online Safety Act 2021
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Gives the eSafety Commissioner removal powers and the ability to register industry codes and make standards. The codes and standards made under it now reach generative AI services, which is how Australia regulates AI-generated harmful material without an AI statute.

records.title: Criminal Code Amendment (Deepfake Sexual Material) Act 2024
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Criminalises transmitting sexual material depicting an adult without consent, including material that has been generated or altered. One of the few Australian statutes written with generative models in view.

records.title: Competition and Consumer Act 2010, Schedule 2 (Australian Consumer Law)
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Misleading or deceptive conduct and the consumer guarantees apply to claims made about AI products and to products that fail because of them. The ACCC has been explicit that overstating what a model does is ordinary consumer law territory, with no AI-specific provision needed.

records.title: Copyright Act 1968
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Australia has fair dealing for specified purposes, not fair use, and no text and data mining exception. Training on copyright material in Australia has a narrower set of defences available than in the United States, which is the central question the Copyright and AI Reference Group was set up to examine.

records.title: Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Risk management obligations for responsible entities in eleven critical sectors. Where an AI system is part of a critical infrastructure asset, the hazard categories and the reporting duties apply to it like anything else.

records.title: Therapeutic Goods Act 1989
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Clinical decision-support and diagnostic software can be a medical device and require TGA inclusion in the Register. This is the one area where an Australian AI developer faces pre-market approval rather than after-the-fact enforcement.

records.title: Corporations Act 2001
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Directors' duties of care and diligence, and the obligation on financial services licensees to provide services efficiently, honestly and fairly, both reach board-level decisions about deploying AI. ASIC has said so directly.

records.title: Digital ID Act 2024
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: Accreditation for digital identity providers, with restrictions on biometric information and on using it for anything beyond verification. Relevant to any face-matching or liveness system operating in the accredited scheme.

records.title: Policy for the responsible use of AI in government
records.force_meaning: Binds government agencies only, not the wider market.
records.note: Mandatory for non-corporate Commonwealth entities from September 2024. Requires an accountable official and a public transparency statement. This is the most concrete binding AI obligation in Australia, and it binds the government rather than the market.

records.title: National framework for the assurance of artificial intelligence in government
records.force_meaning: Binds government agencies only, not the wider market.
records.note: Agreed by Commonwealth, state and territory ministers. Applies the AI Ethics Principles to government use and sets a common assurance approach across jurisdictions, which matters because most public-facing AI in Australia is deployed by states, not the Commonwealth.

records.title: Voluntary AI Safety Standard
records.force_meaning: Guidance with no legal force. Compliance is a choice.
records.body: Department of Industry, Science and Resources
records.note: Ten guardrails covering accountability, risk management, testing, human oversight and disclosure. Written to line up with the mandatory guardrails that were proposed at the same time, so an organisation that adopts it is positioned for legislation that has not arrived.

records.title: Australia's AI Ethics Principles
records.force_meaning: Guidance with no legal force. Compliance is a choice.
records.body: Department of Industry, Science and Resources
records.note: Eight principles, voluntary since 2019. Their practical significance is that later binding government policy adopts them by reference, which gives them force inside the public sector that they do not have outside it.

records.title: National AI Capability Plan
records.force_meaning: Guidance with no legal force. Compliance is a choice.
records.body: Department of Industry, Science and Resources
records.note: The economic strategy rather than the regulatory one: skills, compute, adoption and sovereign capability. Included here because it sets the policy frame the regulatory decisions are being made inside.

records.title: Proposals paper: introducing mandatory guardrails for AI in high-risk settings
records.force_meaning: Proposed, consulted on, or before Parliament. Creates no duties yet.
records.body: Department of Industry, Science and Resources
records.note: Consulted on in late 2024. Proposed a risk-based regime with ten mandatory guardrails and canvassed three options for giving them effect: a new AI act, framework legislation, or amendments to existing law. Nothing has been legislated, which is the single most important fact in this index.

records.title: Guidance on privacy and the use of commercially available AI products
records.force_meaning: How a regulator states it will apply existing law. Creates no obligations of its own.
records.body: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
records.note: What the Australian Privacy Principles require of an organisation buying in a model rather than building one. Includes the OAIC's position that entering personal information into a public generative AI tool is a disclosure.

records.title: Guidance on privacy and developing and training generative AI models
records.force_meaning: How a regulator states it will apply existing law. Creates no obligations of its own.
records.body: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
records.note: The regulator's view on scraping and on training with personal information, including that publicly available does not mean freely usable under the Privacy Act. Directly relevant to anyone training on Australian web data.

records.title: REP 798 Beware the gap: governance arrangements in the face of AI innovation
records.force_meaning: How a regulator states it will apply existing law. Creates no obligations of its own.
records.note: A review of AI use across 23 licensees which found governance lagging deployment. ASIC's position is that existing obligations already bite and that boards cannot wait for AI-specific law.

records.title: Prudential Standard CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
records.force_meaning: Rules, regulations or codes made under an Act. Binding.
records.note: Binding on APRA-regulated entities from July 2025. Requires identification of critical operations and management of material service provider risk, which captures dependence on a third-party model provider.

records.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence Reference Group
records.force_meaning: An inquiry or review. Evidence and recommendations, not obligations.
records.note: The standing forum on whether Australian copyright law needs changing for AI training and AI output. No statutory change has followed, so the Copyright Act as it stands remains the answer.

records.title: Select Committee on Adopting Artificial Intelligence, final report
records.force_meaning: An inquiry or review. Evidence and recommendations, not obligations.
records.note: Recommended that general-purpose models be declared high-risk and that Australia legislate a dedicated AI act. The government has not adopted the recommendation, and the gap between this report and the statute book is worth understanding before reading Australian AI coverage.

records.title: Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme, final report
records.force_meaning: An inquiry or review. Evidence and recommendations, not obligations.
records.note: Not an AI inquiry, and the most important document here for understanding Australian automated decision-making. An automated income-averaging scheme unlawfully raised debts against hundreds of thousands of people. Its recommendations on transparency and on a legislative basis for automated decisions are the reason government AI policy here is as cautious as it is.

records.title: Privacy Act Review Report
records.force_meaning: An inquiry or review. Evidence and recommendations, not obligations.
records.note: 116 proposals, agreed or agreed in principle by the government in 2023. The 2024 amendment act delivered the first tranche; the proposals on automated decisions, a fair and reasonable test, and small business exemptions are still outstanding and would change the AI picture substantially.

records.title: NSW Artificial Intelligence Assessment Framework
records.force_meaning: Binds government agencies only, not the wider market.
records.note: Mandatory for NSW government AI projects and the most developed state-level instrument. Most public-facing government AI in Australia is deployed by states, so Commonwealth policy alone does not describe what citizens meet.

records.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: India's first comprehensive data protection statute. Consent-centred, with narrow exemptions and no explicit automated-decision right. Its rules were notified in stages, so the date it binds a given duty is not the date it passed.

records.title: Information Technology Act 2000
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: The statute everything else is made under, including the intermediary rules. Section 79 safe harbour is the lever the government uses on platforms, and by extension on the generative features inside them.

records.title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021
records.force_meaning: Rules, regulations or codes made under an Act. Binding.
records.body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
records.note: Due diligence duties on intermediaries, amended to reach synthetically generated information and to require it to be labelled. This, not an AI statute, is how India regulates deepfakes.

records.title: India AI Governance Guidelines
records.force_meaning: Guidance with no legal force. Compliance is a choice.
records.body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
records.note: The national framing: govern AI through existing law and institutions rather than a new statute, with voluntary commitments and a techno-legal approach. India's position is closer to the UK's than to the EU's.

records.title: Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI
records.force_meaning: Guidance with no legal force. Compliance is a choice.
records.body: Infocomm Media Development Authority and AI Verify Foundation
records.note: Nine dimensions from accountability and data to incident reporting and security. Voluntary, and widely used as a template outside Singapore, which gives it influence well beyond its legal force.

records.title: Personal Data Protection Act 2012
records.force_meaning: Act of Parliament. Binding on everyone it applies to.
records.note: The binding instrument. Singapore's AI governance work is voluntary; its data protection law is not, and that is where enforcement actually happens.

records.title: Advisory Guidelines on Use of Personal Data in AI Systems
records.force_meaning: How a regulator states it will apply existing law. Creates no obligations of its own.
records.note: How the regulator reads consent, legitimate interests and business improvement exceptions when personal data is used to train or run a model. The operative compliance document for anyone deploying AI in Singapore. Linked to the guidelines index rather than the document, because the PDPC moves its own document URLs and the deep link 404s.

records.title: AI Verify
records.force_meaning: Guidance with no legal force. Compliance is a choice.
records.note: A testing toolkit rather than a document: it runs technical tests and produces a report against the governance principles. Few jurisdictions have turned AI principles into something executable, and this is the clearest attempt.
